items.text: The second edition of the World Humanoid Games kicked off in Beijing, China, and it is showing impressive technological progress in robotics. During the five-day event, a humanoid robot named Lightning even broke Usain Bolt’s 100-meter sprint record, although it struggled to brake after the finish line. Droids also competed in boxing, table tennis, high jump, and household chores like folding laundry. Although advertised as an international event, over 95 percent of the competing companies are Chinese. The games reflect a high-stakes global technology race between China and the United States. While China is currently leading in robotics innovation and using the spectacle as soft power, analysts emphasize that commercial success remains the ultimate goal. Participating companies must perform well to attract investors. The biggest challenge now is transforming these entertaining machines into useful, affordable household products that consumers actually want to buy for daily tasks. Difficult words: brake (to slow down or stop a moving machine, vehicle, or body), droid (a robot, especially one that looks or acts like a human), high-stakes (involving a lot of risk, where you can win or lose a great deal of money or power), spectacle (an impressive, exciting, or unusual public event or show). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The second World Humanoid Games started in Beijing, China. For five days, many robots are competing in sports like boxing, high jump, table tennis, and sprinting. One fast robot even ran 100 meters faster than Usain Bolt. Robots are also practicing household chores , like moving items and folding clothes. Almost all the competing teams come from Chinese companies. China wants to show its high-tech power to the world and compete with the United States. But experts explain that the main goal for these companies is to get money from investors . While these machines can dance and run fast, they are still very expensive and cannot do real housework yet. Chinese companies must now find ways to make useful robots that ordinary people want to buy for their homes. Difficult words: household chore (routine job or task that needs to be done around the house), high-tech (using the most advanced and modern electronic equipment and computers), investor (a person or company that gives money to a business to help it grow and make a profit later). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A big robot event starts in Beijing, China. Robots are competing in running, boxing, jumping, and playing tennis for five days. One robot runs a 100-meter race faster than Usain Bolt. Most of the teams come from Chinese companies. China wants to show new technology to the world. Many children and adults watch the robots dance, fight, and fall. But most companies want to find new investors . These robots cost a lot of money and cannot do real work at home yet. Experts say that companies must build useful robots which people can buy for daily life. Difficult words: compete (to try to be better than someone else), race (an event to see who is the fastest), investor (a person or company that gives money to a business to help it grow and make more money later). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many people receive calls, messages, or emails from someone who is pretending to be a bank or a friend. These scams cost people and countries a lot of money each year. In some countries, criminal gangs build large scam centers to trick people and make money. Some workers go there to earn money, but many are forced to work and face abuse . The gangs use smart methods, such as fake online pictures and messages, to make people give them money. Some workers escape or get help from their countries, but many can’t get away. Governments try to stop the centers, but the gangs have a lot of power and work in areas with weak control. The scams continue because criminals can call people in different places, and the centers teach workers skills to trick people. People need to be careful with calls, messages, and online contacts. Being careful and helping victims can stop some of the harm. Difficult words: pretend (to act like something is true when it is not), scam (a plan to take someone’s money by lying or cheating), abuse (hurting or treating someone very badly). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

People often get calls or messages from someone who says they are a bank or a friend. These scams take money from people all over the world. Some criminal groups make large buildings to trick people. Some workers go there to make money, but others must do it. If they don’t want to, they get hurt. Scammers use fake pictures and messages to make people give them money. Some workers get away or get help from their countries. Governments try to close these buildings, but the criminals have power. They work in many countries. People need to be careful with calls, messages, or online friends. It is the only way they can stop scammers from taking their money. Difficult words: scam (a plan to take someone’s money by lying or cheating), scammer (a person who tries to take money from others by lying), fake (not real). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

People get calls, messages, or emails from someone who wants their money. They say that they are a bank or a friend. We call these people scammers. Scammers make big buildings to trick people. Some workers go there for money. Others cannot leave and get hurt. Scammers use fake pictures and messages to take money. Some workers get help and go home. The police try to close the buildings. It is not easy. Scammers have many buildings in many places. You must be careful. Do not answer strange calls, messages, or friends online. It is a good way to stay safe. Difficult words: trick (to make someone believe something), fake (not real), strange (not usual). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A viral weight-loss transformation trend on TikTok actually uses stolen videos modified by artificial intelligence to sell an app called Her75. At least 11 different accounts posted videos showing identical body movements and framing, but with completely different AI-generated faces. These accounts promoted the app through comments, hashtags, or profile descriptions without clearly labeling their content as commercial advertising. Investigators managed to trace the original clips back to real content creators whose fitness videos were stolen without permission. Experts explained that modern AI tools allow bad actors to quickly perform inexpensive face-swaps and style transfers at a massive scale . Although automated detection software provided mixed results, visual glitches like disappearing hands confirmed the manipulation. When questioned, the app company didn’t respond, but TikTok subsequently removed the accounts for violating community guidelines regarding misleading content, weight-loss claims, and unlabelled advertisements. Difficult words: scale (the size, level, or amount of something, especially when it is very large), glitch (a small, temporary technical fault or mistake in a video or software), subsequently (happening or coming after something else has happened). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A viral weight-loss trend on TikTok uses fake AI videos to sell an app called Her75. Reporters found 11 accounts using the exact same body movements, but with different AI faces. These videos reached millions of views, but they didn’t say they were ads . Investigators traced the clips back to real people whose original videos were stolen. People used modern AI tools to swap faces and change appearances very quickly and cheaply. Small visual mistakes, like strange moving hands, showed that the videos were fake. The app company didn’t answer questions about these posts, but TikTok removed the fake accounts after the investigation. Experts warn that people should carefully check before-and-after videos before trusting products on social media. Difficult words: ad (a picture, video, or text that tries to persuade people to buy a product or service), trace (to find or follow the origin and history of something step by step), appearance (the way that someone or something looks on the outside). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many weight-loss videos on TikTok are fake. Reporters find 11 TikTok accounts which sell an app called Her75. The videos show different women, but they have the same body and move in the same way. People use AI to put new faces on stolen videos from real users. But if you look closely, you can see some mistakes. The app company does not talk to reporters, but TikTok deletes the bad accounts. Experts say that AI makes it very easy to make fake videos. Users should look closely at videos before they buy apps or products online. Difficult words: weight-loss video (a video which shows how someone gets slim), stolen (when someone takes something what is not theirs), delete (to remove information, files, or accounts completely). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Reading is not a natural skill for the human brain. People are born able to see and speak, but they must learn to read. To read, the brain uses parts for seeing, hearing, language, and attention . Reading has developed over thousands of years from early writing like Sumerian symbols and Egyptian pictures to modern letters and words. Reading changes the brain. Letters and words connect to sounds and meanings. All parts of the brain take part in reading. Different languages affect the brain in different ways. For example, Chinese characters use more visual memory than English letters. Learning to read a second language changes the brain differently depending on the writing system. Reading also affects feelings. People can feel the emotions of characters. Reading on phones or tablets often makes people read quickly, which can cause misunderstanding . Children who use screens too much may have trouble focusing and learning. Parents and teachers should help children read deeply, because reading changes the mind and helps people think clearly. Difficult words: attention (the ability to notice or focus on something), visual memory (remembering what you see), misunderstanding (when you don’t understand something correctly). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Reading is not something we are born with. Our brain can see and speak, but we must learn to read letters and words. Reading uses the brain to see, hear, speak, and focus on things. Writing began a long time ago with symbols and pictures, and later became letters and words we use today. Reading changes the brain, but different languages use the brain in different ways. Some languages use memory for pictures more than letters. Learning new languages changes the brain depending on the writing style. Reading can make people feel what they read. Reading on screens can make people only look quickly at words, which can cause mistakes. Children with too much screen time may not focus well. Teachers and parents should help children read a lot to think better. Difficult words: brain (the organ in your head that controls thinking, feeling, and moving), focus (to look at or think about one thing carefully), memory (what you remember). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Babies cannot read. They can see and talk a little, but they must learn to read words and letters. Reading uses the brain for seeing, hearing, talking, and focusing . A long time ago, people use pictures and symbols to write. Later, these become letters as we know them today. Reading changes the brain . Different languages use the brain in different ways. In, some languages you must remember pictures. Learning new languages can change the brain. Reading can make people feel. Reading on phones or tablets can make people read fast and not think well. Children need help from parents and teachers to read a lot and think clearly. Difficult words: focus (to look at or think about one thing carefully), symbol (a picture, or letter which stands for something else), brain (the organ in your head which makes you think, feel, and move). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Global shipping companies are actively searching for alternative routes due to ongoing disruptions in traditional choke points like the Red Sea, Suez Canal, and Panama Canal. A South Korean container ship recently departed from Busan bound for Europe via the Arctic’s Northern Sea Route to test its commercial viability . While the Arctic route offers significantly shorter sailing distances between Asia and Europe, experts are skeptical about its long-term commercial success for containerized goods. Navigating these icy northern waters presents extreme operational challenges, including very narrow summer windows, required ice-strengthened hulls , expensive icebreaker support, and high insurance demands. Furthermore, heavy reliance on Russian territorial permission, nuclear icebreakers, and geopolitical sanctions creates massive hurdles for Western firms. Consequently, analysts emphasize that increased Arctic maritime traffic primarily benefits trade cooperation between Russia and China, rather than providing a widespread solution for Western European supply chains. Difficult words: choke point (a narrow, important place or water passage where movement can be easily blocked or slowed down), viability (the ability of a business idea or plan to work successfully and make a profit), hull (the main outer body or metal frame of a ship that floats in the water). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A South Korean ship is testing a new sailing route through the cold Arctic to carry goods to Europe. Companies want new sea routes because regular paths through the Middle East face serious problems and security threats . The Arctic route is much shorter, but experts say it has many big difficulties. Ships can only sail there for less than three months during the summer when ice melts. Vessels also need special equipment to travel safely through ice, which requires very expensive insurance . Also, ships must get official permission from Russia and use Russian icebreaker ships to help them pass. Because of these safety risks and political problems, most Western companies choose another route. It seems that this Arctic path mostly helps trade between Russia and China. Difficult words: route (a particular way or path taken to get from a starting place to a destination), security threat (a dangerous situation or risk that could cause harm or damage), insurance (an arrangement where you pay money to a company so they pay you back if something gets damaged or lost). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Big ships want new ways to travel because old routes in the Middle East have problems. A ship from South Korea is trying a new sea route through the Arctic to Europe. The Arctic route saves a lot of time because it is shorter. But the water has ice, and ships can only sail there in summer for three months. Ships also need help from Russian icebreaker boats to move through the ice. Because of ice, high costs , and political problems with Russia, many European companies do not want to use this cold route. Right now, this route mostly helps ships trading between Russia and China. Difficult words: route (a way from a starting place to a destination), icebreaker (a strong ship which breaks through ice and clears a path for other boats), costs (the money which you must spend to buy or do something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Over ten thousand people from across Europe and other regions gathered in Berkshire in the United Kingdom for the Medicine Festival. This four-day event combines live music concerts, spiritual awareness , environmental activism , yoga classes, and traditional ceremonies. The sixth edition of the festival highlights the increasing global popularity of conscious festivals. These special gatherings encourage visitors to explore their inner self, reconnect deeply with nature, and build a strong sense of community. Festival co-founder Joshua Dugdale explains that the event promotes the healing power of dance, music, and community, while helping people understand different worldviews and learn new practical skills. Many international visitors traveled long distances to attend the event, hoping to gain inspiration, rest, and personal motivation. Beyond offering unique spiritual experiences, the festival actively supports global causes. To date, Medicine Festival organizers have donated over one hundred thousand euros to protect the natural environment and support indigenous communities. Difficult words: spiritual awareness (a deep mental state of understanding your mind, soul, and connection to life), activism (public work or actions that try to bring about social or political change), indigenous (groups of people who were the original inhabitants of a land before others arrived). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

More than 10,000 people traveled to the United Kingdom to visit the Medicine Festival. This four-day event brings together music, nature, yoga, and traditional ceremonies. It is part of a growing trend of conscious festivals around the world. These events help people connect with nature, think about their inner life, and meet friendly communities. Organizers explain that dance, music, and learning from each other can act like medicine for human health and happiness. Visitors from different countries came to the festival to relax, find new energy, and get inspiration for daily life. The event also cares about important global problems. Until now, the festival has given more than 100,000 euros to protect the environment and help indigenous people. Difficult words: conscious (aware of yourself, your feelings, nature, and the surrounding world), inspiration (a good feeling or new idea which makes you want to do or create something), indigenous (people, plants, or animals which always lived or belonged in a specific place). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many people come to the United Kingdom for a special music event called the Medicine Festival. More than 10,000 visitors join this four-day festival in nature. People do yoga, listen to music, dance, and join traditional ceremonies . This festival helps people relax, feel happy, and meet good friends. Organizers say that nature and music are good for human life. Visitors from different countries come to find new energy and ideas. The festival also loves nature and helps poor people. The organizers give more than 100,000 euros to protect trees, land, and indigenous people around the world. Difficult words: ceremony (a formal event on a special day), organizer (a person who plans and prepares an event or activity), indigenous (people who live in a place for a very long time). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

AI is now part of daily life, from chatbots and photo filters to online customer services. But as AI becomes more advanced , it also helps scammers trick people in new ways. One major threat is deepfake technology, which can clone a person’s voice or face to make fake videos, images, or phone calls that seem completely real. Criminals can use it to ask for money, pretend to be friends, or create fake rental listings. These scams are becoming harder to detect because AI-generated content looks more natural. To stay safe, experts recommend checking the source of information, questioning emotional or shocking messages, and comparing stories on trusted news sites. Watching for unnatural speech or lighting can also help spot AI fakes. Sharing information about scams and staying informed are key to protecting yourself in a world where seeing is not always believing. Difficult words: advanced (very developed or modern), deepfake (realistic fake video or image made by AI), clone (to make an exact copy). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

AI is now everywhere – on phones, websites, and social media. It helps people, but it also gives scammers new ways to lie. One danger is deepfake technology. Scammers can use AI to copy someone’s voice or face and make fake videos or phone calls that look real. They can ask for money or pretend to rent an apartment. These tricks are becoming more difficult to see. To stay safe, people should check where information comes from, think before they act, and look for strange signs like robotic speech or strange faces in videos. Talking about scams with family and friends can also help stop them. Difficult words: scammer (a person who lies to get money), deepfake (realistic fake video or image made by AI), pretend (to act as if something is true when it is not). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

AI is in phones, photos, and websites. It can help people, but some people use it to lie . They can make fake voices and faces. This is called a deepfake . A deepfake can look real. A person can call you and ask for money. But it is not your friend – it is a trick . Some people also make fake photos of houses for rent. To stay safe, check things. Ask, “Who sends this? Why?” If something looks strange, stop and look again. Tell your family or friends if you see a scam. Be careful when you use the internet. Difficult words: lie (to not tell the truth), deepfake (a fake AI video or sound), trick (something that fools someone). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

South Korea celebrated its last traditional hot summer day before a total nationwide ban on dog meat takes effect in February 2027. Following a three-year grace period , the breeding, slaughter, and sale of dogs for human consumption will be strictly illegal, and violators will face fines and prison time. Public opinion has shifted dramatically in recent years due to growing pet ownership and concern for animal welfare . A survey showed that over 80 percent of people supported the ban, while almost 95 percent hadn’t eaten dog meat in the past year. At a market near Seoul, most remaining customers ordering traditional dog meat stew are elderly citizens who believe it boosts stamina . Many businesses are now switching to black goat stew or closing down entirely. Although former merchants acknowledge that stopping the trade is necessary for the country’s international image, many restaurant owners feel sad about losing their loyal, older customers. Difficult words: grace period (extra time allowed before a new law, rule, or payment officially takes effect), welfare (the health, happiness, and comfortable living conditions of people or animals), stamina (the physical strength and energy to keep doing something difficult for a long time). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

South Korea is preparing for a complete ban on dog meat, which starts in February 2027. In the past, many people ate traditional dog meat stew during the hottest days of summer to get more energy. Things are changing, and most South Koreans now support animal welfare and keep pets at home. Surveys show that over 80 percent of people agree with the new law. Today, mainly older people still eat dog meat. Markets are changing, and many restaurants now sell black goat stew instead. Business owners understand that society is changing, but some feel sad for their elderly customers who travel long distances for their favorite traditional meal. The government is planning to help farm owners and sellers move to new businesses. Difficult words: stew (a dish of meat and vegetables cooked slowly together in liquid), welfare (the health and happiness of people or animals), elderly (old people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

South Korea will ban dog meat in February 2027. In the past, people eat dog meat stew on hot summer days. It gives them energy. Today, many people have pets . They love animals, so they do not want to eat dog meat anymore. Most people like the new law. Only old people still visit special markets to eat this traditional food. Many restaurants now sell goat meat instead. Some old restaurant owners are sad. Their long-time customers will miss this meal. But they know that things are changing. The new law is important for the country. Difficult words: stew (a meal when you cook meat and vegetables slowly), pet (an animal which you keep at home for fun), customer (a person who buys things from a shop or business). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Social media feels louder than ever, filled with ads, repetitive videos, and artificial content. At the same time, many people, especially young users, post less or stop completely. A large global study shows social media use drops by about ten percent. This trend has a name: Posting Zero. It means people still look at content, but they choose not to share their own lives online. One reason is that social media no longer feels natural. In the past, people shared simple photos and everyday moments; however, now, feeds look perfect, commercial , and unreal. Many users feel pressure, worry about judgment , or feel guilt when they post happy pictures during wars or disasters. As a result, many prefer silence. Another reason is the rise of bots and fake activity. Much online content now comes from machines, not people, which makes platforms feel empty and less human. Many users hope social media can return to a place where real people share small, honest moments again. Difficult words: artificial (made by people or machines, not natural), commercial (made to sell something or make money), judgment (an opinion about someone or something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The internet feels very loud today, with many ads and repeated videos. At the same time, people post less on social media. A large study from many countries shows social media use goes down, especially among young people. This trend is called Posting Zero. People still watch posts, but they don’t share their own photos or stories. One reason is that social media feels too perfect and too businesslike. In the past, people shared simple daily moments. Now, many users feel stress and worry about how others see them. Some also feel bad about posting happy photos when the world has many problems. Another reason is fake activity online. Many posts and views come from bots , not real people. This makes social media feel less human . Some people hope they can change and feel friendly again. Difficult words: ad (a message that tries to sell a product or service), bot (a computer program that acts like a person), human (a real person, not a machine). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The internet feels very loud . There are many ads and videos. But many people post less on social media. Young people do this most. A big study shows that fewer people share their lives online. This is called Posting Zero. People still look at posts, but they do not post. One reason is that social media feels too perfect. People worry about what others think. Some feel bad when they share happy photos while the world has problems. So they stay quiet. Another reason is fake users. Many posts come from computers, not people. This makes social media feel cold. People want a place where real friends share small, real moments again. Difficult words: loud (very noisy or full of strong messages), ads (a short video to sell something), reason (why something happens). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Sleep deprivation among American teenagers is an epidemic, with only one in ten getting the recommended 8 to 10 hours of sleep per night. The main factor causing this is public policy, specifically early school start times, which force adolescents to wake up hours before their natural biological clock is ready due to a delayed release of the hormone melatonin around puberty. This chronic lack of sleep severely impacts the teenage body and brain. It robs them of essential sleep for learning, memory consolidation , and emotional processing. The consequences are wide-ranging, mimicking ADHD symptoms, irritability, and significantly contributing to mental health issues like increased sadness, hopelessness, and even suicide attempts. Physical health risks, including obesity and diabetes, also rise. Researchers argue that delaying school start times to no earlier than 8:30 am is the unequivocal solution. Districts that have made this change report powerful benefits, including higher test scores, reduced school absences, better mental and physical health, and safer communities due to a sharp drop in teen car crash rates. Difficult words: biological clock (a natural timer inside your body that tells you when you should feel sleepy and when you should feel awake), consolidation (the process of making something stronger and more solid), unequivocal (leaving no doubt; clear). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Sleep deprivation is a big problem for American teenagers, as very few get the 8 to 10 hours of sleep that doctors recommend. The main reason is that many schools start too early, often around 7:30 am, which is not natural to teenagers’ bodies. During puberty, a teen’s natural clock changes, meaning they cannot feel sleepy until about 11 pm. Waking them up at 6 am. is like waking an adult at 4 am. This is the cause of many unpleasant teen behaviors , such as being moody and irritable . It also causes serious health problems like depression and an increased risk of car accidents and diseases. Medical groups say middle and high schools should start no earlier than 8:30 am. Areas which made this change see many benefits: students sleep more, do better in school, don’t skip classes as much, and have better health. Difficult words: sleep deprivation (not getting enough sleep), behavior (the way a person acts), irritable (quickly made angry). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many US teenagers do not get enough sleep. Doctors say that teens need 8 to 10 hours, but most do not get so much. The main reason is that many schools begin lessons too early. When teens grow up, their body clock changes. They feel sleepy later, around 11 pm. Waking a teen up at 6 am. is like waking an adult up at 4 am. Teens are moody . Sleeping little hurts their learning, memory , and feelings. It also causes car crashes. Experts say that schools must start later, after 8:30 am. When schools do this, students sleep more. They get better grades, and they feel happier. The community is safer because there are fewer car accidents. This is the right thing to do for all students. Difficult words: body clock (a natural timer inside your body that tells you when you should feel sleepy and when you should feel awake), moody (when your feelings change often and quickly), memory (remembering things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Europe’s severe drought and heatwaves have caused the Danube River to fall to record lows. Due to a lack of cooling water, Romana has been forced to shut down both reactors at its Cernavoda nuclear power plant. Neighboring Hungary faced a similar crisis at its nuclear facility, which provides 40 percent of the nation’s power. Extreme summer temperatures have shifted peak electricity demand from winter to summer as households rely heavily on air conditioning. Fortunately, Hungary avoided major power shortages because of a massive sixfold increase in solar energy production over the last five years, which covered up to 90 percent of daytime power needs. However, meeting evening electricity demand remains a significant challenge. Environmental experts warn that growing electricity needs from air conditioning, data centers, and electric vehicles are putting immense strain on energy systems. They emphasize that European policymakers must quickly adapt critical infrastructure to handle unprecedented climate extremes that threaten energy, water, and food security. Difficult words: shortage (a situation in which there is not enough of something people need), sixfold (six times as much or as many), strain (severe pressure or worry placed on a system, person, or object). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Severe drought and hot summer weather have caused big problems in Europe. The water level in the Danube River is very low, so Romania had to stop its nuclear power plant because there was not enough cold water. Nearby Hungary also had water problems at its nuclear plant. Hot weather makes people use more air conditioning , which needs a lot of electricity. Luckily, Hungary uses much more solar power now, which helped supply energy during hot daytime hours, but getting enough power during the night is still difficult. Experts say that energy demand is growing because of electric cars and cooling systems. They warn that European governments must prepare better for extreme weather to keep energy, water, and food supplies safe for everyone in the future. Difficult words: drought (a long period of time with little or no rain), air conditioning (a system used to cool down the air in a building or vehicle), supply (an amount of something people can use). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Hot weather and low rainfall cause big problems in Europe. Danube is the biggest river in Romania. It has very low water levels now. Romania must stop its nuclear power plant . The plant needs water to cool down. In Hungary, people use a lot of electricity for air conditioning during hot summer days. Luckily, solar power helps make electricity when the sun shines. But it is still hard to get power at night. Experts say that people are using more energy for cars, data centers, and cooling. Countries must plan better to protect their water and power for the future . Difficult words: nuclear power plant (a factory which breaks atoms to make energy), air conditioning (a system which makes a room or house cold on a hot day), future (the time after now). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Millions of people across Europe witnessed a spectacular solar eclipse that marked the most significant astronomical event the region has experienced since 1999. While viewers in Iceland and northern Spain were treated to a total eclipse, onlookers across the United Kingdom experienced a dramatic partial eclipse, with the moon blocking up to 96% of the sun in places like Cornwall. Stargazers gathered in large crowds along coastlines, city monuments, and hills, and wore protective solar glasses to watch the sun transform into a thin crescent . As the peak moment arrived, day turned into darkness, temperatures dropped noticeably, and streetlights turned on, which created an eerie atmosphere for observers. Scientists and travelers described witnessing the sun’s shimmering corona and nuclear explosions as an unforgettable, humbling experience that reminded them of humanity’s small place in the cosmos. Experts note that a total eclipse will not be visible from the UK again until 2090. Difficult words: onlooker (a person who watches an event or activity taking place without taking part in it), stargazer (a person who enjoys looking at the night sky, stars, and planets), crescent (a thin, curved shape that is thick in the middle and pointed at both ends), eerie (strange, mysterious, and a little scary). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Millions of people in Europe watched an amazing solar eclipse in the sky. It was the best eclipse seen in the region since 1999. People in Spain and Iceland saw a total eclipse, where the moon completely covered the sun and made the land dark. In the UK, the moon blocked most of the sun and left only a thin shape in the sky. Crowds of people gathered outside with special protective glasses to watch the rare event together. During the peak moment, the sky became dark, the air felt cold, and city lights came on during the daytime. Scientists and tourists were very excited to see this rare event. Experts say that people in the UK will have to wait until 2090 to see another total solar eclipse like this one again. Difficult words: eclipse (an event where one space object blocks the light of another space object), protective glasses (special glasses which protect your eyes from injury or bright light), peak (the highest point, strongest moment, or top level of something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Millions of people in Europe look at the sky to see a solar eclipse . The moon moves in front of the sun and blocks its light. In Spain and Iceland, the sky becomes very dark, like night. In the UK, people see only a small part of the sun in the sky. Many people go outside together. They wear special glasses to stay safe. During the eclipse, the air gets cold, and the light is low. People are very happy and excited to watch this special event. Experts say that this is a very rare day. People in the UK will wait a long time to see it again. The next solar eclipse will be in 2090. Difficult words: solar eclipse (when the moon passes between the sun and Earth and blocks the sun’s light), excited (very happy and full of energy about something), rare (when something happens very seldom). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Bubble tea, also known as boba, has become a global phenomenon , loved for its colorful look and sweet taste. Originating in Taiwan in the 1980s, it mixes tea, milk, sugar, and tapioca pearls. Social media helped turn it into a popular trend, but now experts are warning about health risks. Tests in the United States found small amounts of lead in tapioca pearls, made from cassava that absorbs heavy metals from soil. Although the levels are low, repeated exposure may be harmful. Doctors also warn that drinking bubble tea too often can cause digestive problems, kidney stones, and obesity due to its high sugar content, sometimes up to 50 grams per cup. Some pearls can even cause choking, especially in children. Experts suggest smaller cups, less sugar, and water instead of sweet drinks. Bubble tea is safe in moderation, but unhealthy as a daily habit. Difficult words: phenomenon (something very popular or remarkable), tapioca (a small soft ball from a plant called cassava), cassava (a tropical root plant; its starch is used to make tapioca). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Bubble tea is a sweet drink from Taiwan. It has tea, milk, sugar, and soft balls called tapioca pearls. The drink became famous on social media, and people can buy it all around the world. But doctors are worried about its health effects. Tests in the United States found small amounts of lead in tapioca pearls. They come from cassava , which can take heavy metals from the soil. Too much bubble tea can cause stomach pain, kidney stones, and obesity. It also has a lot of sugar, more than a cola. Some people can even choke on the pearls. Health experts say to drink less, take smaller cups, and choose water when thirsty. Difficult words: tapioca (a small soft ball from a plant), lead (a heavy metal that can be toxic), cassava (a tropical plant), choke (to have something block your throat so you cannot breathe properly). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Germany is actively working to expand its military, increase weapons production, and recruit more young soldiers amid growing European fears of potential Russian military action and shifting US security policies. The government has launched a massive 80 million dollar recruitment campaign, using public ads, direct mail, and even free kebab wrapping paper to attract young adults. Authorities have sent out over 300,000 registration letters asking young men about their physical fitness and willingness to fight. However, these recruitment efforts are meeting strong resistance from German youth. Only 530 people have signed up so far, while nearly 6,000 individuals have registered as conscientious objectors this year to refuse military service. Thousands of students have organized school walkouts and street protests against rearmament plans. While about 70 percent of German citizens support increasing defense spending, many young people strongly object to military service. This raises serious questions about whether the nation can successfully recruit the 80,000 additional troops it currently needs. Difficult words: resistance (fighting or speaking out against something you do not agree with), conscientious objector (a person who officially refuses to join the military or fight in a war because of their personal moral or religious beliefs), rearmament (the process of building up a country’s supply of weapons and military forces again). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Germany wants to grow its military because of security worries in Europe. The government needs 80,000 new soldiers, so it is spending millions of dollars on advertisements to invite young people to join. Officials sent hundreds of thousands of letters to teenagers to check their fitness and interest in fighting. But very few young men want to join the army. Many teenagers say they prefer to study and don’t want to fight for the military. Almost 6,000 young Germans officially refused to serve as soldiers this year, which is a big increase from past years. Students are also organizing protests against army plans in schools and streets. Although most adults support spending money on defense , finding enough young people who are willing to become soldiers remains a big problem for Germany. Difficult words: refuse (to say clearly that you will not do or accept something), defense (actions, weapons, or systems used to protect a country or person from an attack), willing (ready or happy to do something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Difficult words: army (a large group of people who fight on land), ad (a picture, text, or video which tries to make people buy or do something), agree (to say yes to a plan or idea). Imagine you discover a potion that makes you immortal . Drinking it would freeze your body at its current age, protect you from disease, and ensure survival for as long as the universe exists. The main question is: would you drink it? Some philosophers see immortality as full of exciting possibilities. You could explore endlessly, pursue long-term goals, and never fear death. John Martin Fischer argues that certain pleasures, like watching sunsets, would stay enjoyable, and personal or social ambitions could always provide meaning. Others believe immortality has serious problems. Bernard Williams warns that life would eventually become unbearably monotonous, with repeated activities losing their charm . He also argues that constant change in values and identity could make life unstable, even meaningless. Samuel Scheffler adds that time limits are what make human life valuable: knowing we will die pushes us to make choices. For many, eternal life might be more of a curse than a blessing. Difficult words: potion (a drink with special power, often in stories), immortal (living forever, never dying), charm (something that makes people like it or find it attractive), curse (a bad spell or power that brings harm). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

If you find a potion that gives you eternal life, would you drink it? The potion keeps you young, safe from disease, and alive forever. Some philosophers say immortality brings freedom. You could travel, try new hobbies, and reach many goals without worrying about time. John Martin Fischer says some things, like sunsets, never get old. But other philosophers warn of problems. Bernard Williams says life would turn boring after repeating the same activities for centuries. Changing your habits and identity again and again could also feel confusing. Samuel Scheffler adds that limited time gives life meaning, because we must decide what is important before we die. Eternal life, therefore, could feel like both a gift and a problem. Difficult words: potion (a drink with special power, often in stories), eternal (lasting forever, with no end), immortality (living forever, never dying). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

You find a magic potion . If you drink it, you will live forever. You cannot get sick, and your body will stay the same age. Some people think that this is very good. You can do many things, travel, and still learn something new. You never need to be afraid of death. But some people think that it is not good. Bernard Williams says that life can get boring if you repeat the same things for many years. Samuel Scheffler says that life is special because it is short. When we know that time is not forever, we choose what is important. With no end, life may lose meaning . Living forever can be both happy and sad. Difficult words: magic (special power which changes things in a way which we cannot explain), potion (a drink with special power, often in stories), meaning (important quality why we do things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Indonesia is currently facing a severe waste crisis as many of its landfills reach full capacity. The largest site, Bantargebang near Jakarta, covers more than 100 hectares and has piled up garbage as high as a 16-storey building. This massive landfill poses constant danger to nearby communities and thousands of informal workers due to toxic methane fires and frequent trash landslides. Following a tragic landslide in March that killed seven people, the Indonesian government promised major reforms. Authorities plan to end unrestricted open dumping, reshape steep slopes, improve drainage systems, and mandate waste sorting so landfills eventually receive only residual waste . However, these changes worry thousands of informal waste collectors who survive by searching through garbage to resell items for a few dollars a day. While workers fear losing their daily income, government officials promise to create safer, formal jobs in newly planned processing facilities to separate recyclable materials properly. Difficult words: drainage (a system of pipes or channels that carries water or liquid waste away from an area), mandate (to make an official rule or order that forces people to do something), residual waste (trash that cannot be recycled, reused, or composted and must be thrown away). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Indonesia has a very big trash problem because many landfills are full. Near Jakarta, the biggest landfill is 65 meters high, like a tall building. Working there is dangerous because of hot fires and trash landslides. In March, a large garbage collapse killed seven workers. Now, the government wants to stop open dumping and make landfills safer. Officials plan to clean up the slopes, build better water systems, and ask people to sort their trash before throwing it away. Thousands of poor workers are worried about these changes. They make money by finding and selling old plastic or metal items from the trash. The government promises that the new laws will create better, safer jobs at new recycling plants to help everyone. Difficult words: landfill (a large public area where garbage is buried under the ground or piled up into mountains), collapse (falling down suddenly), open d umping (leaving trash in open fields or unmanaged areas without protective covers or safety controls). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In the early 2000s, invasive big-headed ants arrived in Kenya’s Laikipia Plateau, probably through imported goods. These ants formed huge super-colonies, hunting insects, spiders, and even birds. Their arrival disrupted the ecosystem, particularly the relationship between whistling-thorn acacia trees and their protective acacia ants. Normally, acacia ants defend the trees against herbivores like elephants by swarming and biting. However, big-headed ants killed native ants and destroyed their nests. Without this protection, acacia trees became weak, lost leaves, and collapsed more often. This changed the savannah landscape, leaving fewer trees and more open grasslands. The new environment affected lions’ hunting strategies. Lions usually prefer zebras, which they ambush in tree-rich areas. With fewer trees, zebras escaped more easily, so lions increasingly targeted dangerous buffalo instead. This chain reaction shows how a tiny invasive species can transform an ecosystem, influencing plants, insects, and even top predators like lions. Difficult words: disrupt (to stop something from working normally), swarm (to move together in a large group, usually busily or aggressively), ambush (to wait and attack someone or an animal suddenly, usually from a hidden place). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Big-headed ants came to Kenya’s Laikipia Plateau in the 2000s and spread quickly. They attacked many insects and birds, but the biggest problem was their fight with local acacia ants. Acacia ants live inside whistling-thorn acacia trees and protect them from animals like elephants. The new ants killed acacia ants and made the trees weak. Many trees fell, and the land became open grassland. This change also influenced lions. Lions usually hunt zebras, but they need trees to hide before jumping on them. When trees disappeared , zebras ran away more easily. Lions then started to hunt more buffalo, which are stronger and more dangerous. In this way, very small ants changed plants, trees, and even the food of lions. Difficult words: influence (to affect someone or something), hide (to put something or yourself in a place where others cannot see it), disappear (to go away or into a place where others cannot see you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Then the trees are not strong, and many trees fall. The land has fewer trees and more grass. This is bad for lions. Lions need trees to hide when they hunt zebras. With no trees, zebras run away. Lions start to hunt buffalo, but buffalo are big and hard to catch. Difficult words: insects (a small animal with six legs), bite (to use your teeth to cut or hold something), hide (to put something or yourself in a place where others cannot see it). Two famous UNESCO World Heritage sites in Latin America are facing serious threats from human activity and climate change. In Peru, the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu receives nearly 1.8 million visitors every year. Heavy foot traffic is eroding fragile stone structures, while extreme weather, melting glaciers, and severe waste management issues cause further environmental damage. Authorities have introduced a four-year master plan to restrict daily visitor numbers to 5,600 and improve waste treatment. Meanwhile, Honduras’ Rio Plátano Biosphere Reserve, Central America’s largest remaining rainforest, is severely threatened by illegal cattle ranching, illegal logging, gold mining, and drug trafficking. Deforestation is destroying ecosystems, archaeological ruins, and local wildlife, while indigenous leaders face violent threats for defending their lands. According to UNESCO officials, saving these irreplaceable treasures requires urgent international cooperation, better funding, and strict enforcement . Local communities, archaeologists, and global organizations must work together closely to protect these historical and natural monuments before they are lost forever. Difficult words: citadel (strong fortress or castle built high up to protect a city), fragile (easy to break, damage, or destroy), enforcement (making sure that people obey rules or laws). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Machu Picchu in Peru and the Rio Plátano Biosphere Reserve in Honduras are famous UNESCO sites under danger. In Peru, millions of tourists visit Machu Picchu every year. Too many visitors walk on the ancient stone paths, which causes damage and erosion . Heavy rain, changing weather, and trash also create big problems. Local authorities now limit daily visitors to protect the area. In Honduras, large parts of the rainforest are being destroyed by illegal cattle farming, tree cutting, and drug crime. This dangerous activity harms wild animals and threatens local communities. Indigenous leaders try to protect their forest homes, but armed groups hurt them. Experts say that governments, local people, and international organizations must work together to save these special cultural and natural places for the future. Difficult words: ancient (very old), erosion (the slow wearing away of earth, rock, or stone by wind, water, or traffic), indigenous (living in a place from the very beginning). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Two famous places in Latin America are in big danger today. Machu Picchu in Peru has too many tourists every year. Many people walk on old stones and damage the site . Bad weather and heavy rain also cause big problems. The government now limits how many people can visit each day. In Honduras, people cut down big trees in a famous rainforest. Illegal farms, gold mining , and criminals destroy the forest and harm wild animals. Local people try to save their land, but it is dangerous. Experts say that countries must work together now to help save these special nature sites. Difficult words: site (a specific place where something is located), limit (the maximum number or amount which is still possible), mining (digging into the ground to get metals). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Finland, blueberries are more than a healthy snack; they are part of the national culture. Thanks to the so-called everyman’s right, people can freely enter forests and collect berries if they don’t disturb others. Each summer, families head out together, and knowledge about the best blueberry spots often passes from one generation to the next. Blogger Varpu Rusila explains that picking blueberries is both a tradition and a way to appreciate nature. Blueberries appear everywhere in Finnish life. They are in breakfast porridge, smoothies, ice cream, and the famous mustikkapiirakka, or blueberry pie. Families prepare simple recipes at home, often using wild blueberries because they are smaller, tastier, and richer in nutrients than farmed ones. Blueberries are also part of daily life in Helsinki, where people enjoy blueberry products in markets, cafés, and restaurants. The fruit is seen as both food and a cultural symbol. For Finns, blueberry picking connects health, family, and their close relationship with forests. Difficult words: spot (a place or location), appreciate (to be thankful for something or to see its value), nutrient (a substance that helps the body grow and stay healthy). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In Finland, blueberries are not only food but also an important part of life. People can go into forests and pick berries freely . Families go together each summer, and children learn the best places from their parents. Blogger Varpu Rusila says blueberry picking is a way to enjoy nature. Blueberries are in many dishes. People use them in porridge , smoothies, ice cream, and blueberry pie. Finns usually choose wild blueberries because they are small, dark, and full of taste and vitamins. In Helsinki, blueberries are everywhere. Shops, cafés, and markets sell products with blueberries. For Finns, blueberries give both health and happiness, and they show the strong connection between people and nature. Difficult words: freely (without limit), porridge (soft food made by cooking oats in water or milk), connection (a link between two things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

They put them in porridge , pie, ice cream, and smoothies. Wild blueberries are small and very tasty. They also help people stay strong and healthy. In Helsinki, people see blueberries in many places. Shops and cafés sell food with blueberries. For Finnish people, blueberries mean health, family time, and love for the forest. Difficult words: freely (without limit or rule), nature (the world of trees, animals, land, and so on), porridge (soft food when you cook oats in water or milk). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Saunas have been part of human culture for thousands of years, from Finnish sauna traditions to Japanese onsen and Indigenous sweat lodges. Modern science is now studying their effects on health. A long-term Finnish study of over 2,000 men found that frequent sauna use was linked to better heart health, lower blood pressure, healthier cholesterol, and reduced risk of death. Saunas reach up to 90°C with low humidity, triggering the body’s thermoregulatory system: blood vessels widen, heart rate rises, skin absorbs heat, and sweating cools the body. This reaction is similar to moderate exercise, which may strengthen the cardiovascular system. Sauna use may also aid muscle recovery after workouts by improving blood flow, reducing excess inflammation , and helping the body clear waste. Another benefit is the production of heat shock proteins, which repair DNA and support cell health. However, scientists caution that research is still limited to certain groups and lifestyles, and high heat may be unsafe for some people, such as those with health conditions. Difficult words: thermoregulatory (controlling body temperature), cardiovascular (related to the heart and blood vessels), inflammation (the body’s natural reaction to injury or infection, often causing pain or swelling). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

People started using saunas and hot baths thousands of years ago, but scientists are only now learning how they affect health. A Finnish study of more than 2,000 men showed that those who used saunas often were healthier, with lower blood pressure, better cholesterol, and less risk of dying early. In a sauna, the heat up to 90°C makes your heart beat faster, your blood vessels open, and your body sweat . This looks like exercise, and it may make the heart stronger. Saunas may also help muscles recover after sports by improving blood flow and reducing inflammation . Heat can also increase special proteins that repair cells. Still, scientists say saunas are not safe for everyone, and there needs to be more research to know all the benefits and limits. Difficult words: vessel (a tube in your body through which blood travels), sweat (when your skin gets wet after an exercise or when you are hot), inflammation (the body’s reaction to injury or infection). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Saunas are hot rooms which people use for health and relaxation . They are old traditions in many countries, like Finland and Japan. Scientists study 2,000 Finnish men. They find that people who go to saunas often are healthier. They have lower blood pressure , better heart health, and live longer. In a sauna, the heat up to 90°C makes you sweat , your heart beat faster, and your blood move quickly. This is like doing exercise. Saunas may also help tired muscles after sport and make the body stronger. Heat can also help repair cells in the body. But saunas are not safe for everyone, for example, pregnant women or those with health problems. Difficult words: relaxation (when you rest and feel calm), blood pressure (the power your blood goes through your body), sweat (when your skin gets wet after an exercise or when you are hot). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
